newsitem.title: USA: Rubin warns against rosy talk of budget surpluses.
newsitem.headline: Rubin warns against rosy talk of budget surpluses.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had a message on Thursday for lawmakers and pundits already dreaming of ways the government can spend a budget surplus: Don't count your chickens before they're hatched.
"We have a lot to do between here and the day we have a surplus," Rubin told Reuters in an interview. "A lot of difficult decisions have to be made."

President Clinton and the Republican-led Congress this week struck a landmark agreement to balance the $1.5 trillion federal budget by the year 2002 -- the first time that the government will not be in the red since 1969.

But some lawmakers are not stopping there and are already scrapping with each other over what to do when the budget runs a surplus, with some advocating tax cuts, others spending increases and still others, reductions in government debt.

Rubin made clear that he thought that such talk was premature. In order to ensure that the agreement struck this week actually balances the budget, Congress and the Clinton administration still must make tough decisions each year on spending priorities, he said.
Washington must also tackle the problem of the mounting costs of such entitlement programmes as Medicare, Rubin said.
The budget agreement trims spending on the Medicare health programme for the aged by $115 billion over five years and sets up a bipartisan commission to study further possible reforms.

Rubin said "some kind of commission-like vehicle" will probably also be set up to look at the problems facing the government's Social Security pension programme in the next century as the baby boom generation reaches retirement.

Some experts have criticised this week's agreement for not doing more to rein in entitlement spending and have argued that the budget would have been balanced on its own without the pact, as a strong economy boosted government tax revenues.
Rubin took issue with critics and defended the agreement.
"Within the realm of the practical, we really took it as far as we could go," he said, adding, "It is a very substantial accomplishment."

While the budget deficit in the current fiscal year ending on Sept. 30 looks to be coming at under $50 billion, the red ink would not disappear in future years on its own without this week's agreement, Rubin said.
